raw_case_text: A 32-year-old woman, a known case of idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy with progressive heart failure presented with New York Heart Association class 3-4 heart failure and underwent orthotopic heart transplantation (HTx). Her immunosuppressant regimen included anti-thymocyte globulin, prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, and tacrolimus. Her post-operative course was uneventful and she was discharged in excellent condition on 12th post-operative day. Four months later, she presented with dry cough of two days duration. The patient denied any fever, chills, hemoptysis, chest pain, myalgia, orthopnea, and palpitation. Vital signs included a blood pressure of 120/70 mm Hg, oral temperature of 37.2  C, heart rate of 78 beats/min, respiratory rate of 18 breath/min, and O2 saturation of 94% at room temperature. In physical examination, normal heart sounds and clear breathing sounds were noted. Laboratory blood tests showed total white blood cell count of 8200/mm3, 65% neutrophils, 28% lymphocyte, 4% monocytes and 3% eosinophils. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) was negative. Renal and liver function tests were within normal range. Chest x-ray was normal (Fig 1). An echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 50%, which was unchanged from the previous results. After six hours, she developed dyspnea and low-grade fever. Repeated chest x-ray revealed a new infiltration involving the right-middle and lower lobes (Fig 2). On suspicion of pneumonia, bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage were performed. Blood, urine, and stool culture were obtained and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy was initiated. Computed tomography of chest revealed bilateral multiple well-defined consolidations with halo sign (Fig 3). At this stage, clinical diagnosis of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis was made and antifungal therapy was initiated with voriconazole and amphotericin B. Prednisolone was discontinued. The immunosuppressant doses were lowered. Serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen assay was requested. The condition of the patient worsened; she developed sudden-onset respiratory failure, necessitating endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Her hemodynamic became unstable, requiring vasopressor support. After two more hours the patient worsened clinically and subsequently succumbed to cardiorespiratory arrest. Blood, urine, and stool cultures showed no microbial growth after four days of incubation. The test for CMV antigenemia was negative. Multiple bronchoalveolar lavage cultures isolated A. fumigatus.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old female heart transplant recipient presented 4 months post-transplantation with a 2-day history of dry cough, followed 6 hours after admission by acute dyspnea and low-grade fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Four months after an uneventful orthotopic heart transplant for NYHA class III-IV idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy (maintained on prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, and tacrolimus after ATG induction), the patient presented with a 2-day history of isolated dry cough and a normal initial chest X-ray. Six hours after admission, she acutely developed dyspnea, low-grade fever, and new right middle and lower lobe infiltrates, rapidly progressing within hours to hypoxemic respiratory failure, shock, and fatal cardiorespiratory arrest.
subjective.past_medical_history: Idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy status post orthotopic heart transplantation 4 months prior; immunosuppressive regimen included anti-thymocyte globulin induction and maintenance prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, and tacrolimus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dry cough (2 days), followed by acute dyspnea and low-grade fever; negative on arrival for chills, hemoptysis, chest pain, myalgia, orthopnea, or palpitations.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission vitals: blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, oral temperature 37.2 C, heart rate 78 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and SpO2 94% on room air, with clear lung sounds and normal heart sounds. Six hours later, she developed low-grade fever, acute respiratory distress, and subsequent hemodynamic collapse requiring mechanical ventilation and vasopressors.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs were normal: WBC 8,200/mm3 (65% neutrophils, 28% lymphocytes, 4% monocytes, 3% eosinophils), normal renal and liver function tests, and negative CMV testing and CMV antigenemia. Blood, urine, and stool cultures remained sterile after 4 days. Echocardiogram showed a stable LVEF of 50%. Initial chest X-ray was normal, but repeat chest X-ray 6 hours later showed new right middle and lower lobe infiltrates.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated multiple well-defined bilateral pulmonary consolidations with surrounding ground-glass halo signs. Diagnostic bronchoscopy with multiple bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cultures isolated Aspergillus fumigatus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Fulminant invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus) presenting 4 months after orthotopic heart transplantation with rapid progression from a normal chest radiograph to fatal cardiorespiratory arrest within hours, confirmed by bilateral halo-sign consolidations on chest CT and isolation of A. fumigatus from multiple BAL cultures. Despite immediate reduction of immunosuppression (stopping prednisolone), empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics, combination antifungal therapy with voriconazole and amphotericin B, mechanical ventilation, and vasopressors, the patient succumbed to cardiorespiratory arrest.
